pr_title: kvprober: dump traces of all probes to a dedicated logging channel
pr_body:
**kvprober: dump traces of all probes to a dedicated logging channel**
    
This commit dumps traces of all probes sent by kvprober to a dedicated logging
channel. Today, CC does not have proper tracing infra set up. Still, having
traces of probes simplifies production debugging. For now, a simple text
file full of such traces will do, and the default configuration for the new
logging channel implies producing exactly that.
    
Note that we can consider phasing this out, once CC has proper tracing infra to
which we can send traces.
    
It appears that with a 100MB retention size, one read probe per second, & one
write probe per five seconds, we store ~N=200 minutes worth of traces. This
might be sufficent, especially given that this is a stopgap. Of course, we can
always increase the retention size of this one channel across the CC fleet.
    
This should be considered for 21.2 backport. Note that kvprober is off by
default & behind private cluster settings.
    
Fixes #69427.
    
Release note (ops change): kvprober is an off by default component guarded by
private cluster settings. kvprober sends probes to KV to measure availabilty.
This commit updates kvprober to write traces to a new logging channel, which
goes to a file in the logs dir by default.

CC @dhartunian @tbg

issue_context.title: tracing: export kvprober traces to a dedicated log file
issue_context.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
Currently, traces can only be exported wholesale to external tracing aggregation services. This makes it difficult to just look at traces from the kvprober which can more reliably pinpoint range-related issues.

**Describe the solution you'd like**
We would like to add the ability to export all kvprober traces to a dedicated log file. Similarly to the slow query log, this should be a separate file from the rest of the logs that collects all the kvprober logs and trace timings.

This feature should be gated with a cluster setting that enables or disables trace exporting to a file.

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
A more generalized tracing categorization/persistence method is too complex to design and build at the moment.
Exporting the traces to a 3rd party is a good idea but CC has no infra to send traces to ATM, and this will take time to build out, time no CC team has right now.

Jira issue: CRDB-9592

review_comments:
FWIW, one way I imagined this stuff could work is to have a `heap_profiler` for such traces. That is, instead of (or in addition to) dumping walls of text into the logs, we have a [Dumper](https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/blob/a74d71d895980281d7dabec26711b274811d8727/pkg/server/dumpstore/dumpstore.go#L51) somewhere that takes kvprober traces and writes them out in [Jaeger format](https://github.com/cockroachdb/cockroach/blob/775c2b0b0302ebf4b0c8c8515e015b793b8585ce/pkg/util/tracing/recording.go#L322-L328), where they can easily be explored (using [jaeger](https://www.jaegertracing.io/)).

I think this use case inverts what the Dumper was made for somewhat - the dumper does action X every Y seconds and grooms the result set - here it gets handed something at arbitrary points in time and grooms - but I think it could be accommodated.

This might be too big a lift for @joshimhoff but perhaps we can discuss the idea here. The proposed mechanism for trace collection would also be helpful for #33007 and I am sure we would find a few more places where it ends up helpful; for example once we are at the place where we can start tracing requests that are "slow", the trace has to be collected somewhere as well.

I like this idea a lot!

> I think this use case inverts what the Dumper was made for somewhat - the dumper does action X every Y seconds and grooms the result set - here it gets handed something at arbitrary points in time and grooms - but I think it could be accommodated.

Yes we can alter the design to make the retention policy more flexible.
